title: Going to the baths
hook: before going out, picture what happens at the public baths: splashing, shoving, theft, and keep your purpose (Enchiridion 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus and the jug. Your line was clay breaks; that's part of what clay is. Did something small break or spill, and did you say the line first? Day three hundred thirty-six, the end of a week.
screen: `CLAY BREAKS; THAT'S PART OF WHAT CLAY IS.`

segments.voice: A public bathhouse, a busy afternoon. Steam, echoing tile, a hundred voices. Somebody cannonballs into the pool and soaks your towel. Somebody shoves past you on the wet steps. Somebody shouts insults across the room. And somebody, while you're in the water, walks off with your sandals. None of it is strange for a crowded bath; it is simply what happens there. This is the scene Epictetus chooses for section four. Not a battlefield. An afternoon errand. Today: going to the baths.
screen: `STEAM, TILE, A HUNDRED VOICES.` → `SPLASHED, SHOVED, ROBBED.` → `GOING TO THE BATHS.`

segments.voice: First, the preview. When you're about to do anything, Epictetus says, remind yourself what kind of activity it is. If you're going out to bathe, picture what happens at the baths: people who splash you, people who push, people who insult you, people who steal. Nothing mysterious. Just honest weather for that place. Second, the sentence you carry in. Having pictured it, say to yourself: I want to bathe, and to keep my purpose in line with nature. Notice the and. You're not going only for a bath. You're going for a bath and to stay the kind of person you mean to be while you're there. Third, the payoff. Then, he says, if something gets in the way of your bath, you'll have the words ready: I didn't want only to bathe, but also to keep my purpose, and I won't keep it if I'm furious about every splash. The bath can go badly and the trip can still succeed, because half of what you came for was always yours. Fourth, today's bathhouse. The grocery store at six. The family dinner where a certain uncle will say a certain thing. The group chat. The morning commute. None of it is a surprise, and yet it can still ambush us, because we walk in expecting only the errand. A one-minute preview at the door, and an and attached to the errand, changes what counts as a good outing. And a look back at the week. Year two opened with a book for the hand, then two piles, then desire held lightly, a jug, and today the baths. Each one is small enough to carry out the door.
screen: `PICTURE WHAT HAPPENS THERE.` · `I WANT TO BATHE, AND KEEP MY PURPOSE.` · `THE BATH FAILS, THE TRIP SUCCEEDS.` · `TODAY'S BATHHOUSE.` · then, large: `AND KEEP MY PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Choose one outing ahead of you today or tomorrow. A store, an office, a visit, a phone call. Close your eyes and walk through it. Who'll be there? What usually goes wrong? The line, the delay, the comment, the noise. Let each one appear without bracing. Then say your sentence inside: I want to do this errand, and keep my purpose. Picture yourself in the middle of the worst moment, still steady. The bell holds the time.
Epictetus, previewing an errand: picture what usually happens, then go with two aims, the errand and your own purpose. Today's word.
Your line: and keep my purpose. Before you walk through one door today, add those words to whatever you came for. A week of year two done. Day three hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners take a moment before an outing to picture its usual frustrations and name their aim: to do the errand and stay the person they mean to be.

original.note: Greek, Enchiridion 4: a bath, a bathhouse.

trapdoor: what you thought: expect the worst so you're not disappointed.
what it means: picture what the place is usually like, then go with two aims, the errand and your purpose.
what a scholar hears: 'in line with nature' (kata phusin) is the Stoic phrase; the purpose is prohairesis, the will, the one thing Epictetus calls truly ours.
recall: knowing the limits of what you can know

notes: Review (2026-10-01): hook opened with the banned 'Picture'; removed the unsourced claim about bathhouse theft and curse tablets (and its myth item and source); softened 'ambushes us every time'.
Enchiridion 4 paraphrased (splashing, pushing, abusing, stealing; 'I will bathe and keep my will in accord with nature'). Confirm.

Curse tablets about stolen clothing at baths: the best-known set comes from Aquae Sulis (Bath, England), from the Roman period; confirm the general claim 'curse tablets asking the gods to punish whoever took their cloak'.
Greek βαλανεῖον: confirm it is the word used in Enchiridion 4 (the text uses λούσασθαι for 'to bathe' and refers to τὰ ἐν βαλανείῳ).
Trapdoor: kata phusin and prohairesis; confirm.
